title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Metabolomics measures small molecules in biofluids and tissues and provides a high-dimensional readout of endogenous metabolism plus the exogenous inputs (e.g., diet, drugs, pollutants, microbiome-derived metabolites). In nutritional epidemiology, it is increasingly used to: (i) improve dietary exposure assessment, (ii) identify mechanistic pathways linking diet to disease, and (iii) support metabolic phenotyping relevant for precision prevention.
An additional motivation is that self-reported diet instruments (e.g., FFQs, recalls) introduce substantial measurement error because they rely on memory, social desirability, and imperfect reporting (including under- or over-reporting), which can attenuate diet–disease associations and bias inference. Metabolomics has the potential to objectively measure intake, leveraging and/or substituting traditional assessment.
Key study designs in the field:

Controlled dietary interventions: strongest for causal attribution and biomarker discovery.
Prospective cohorts: strong for disease prediction and mediation pathways (but confounding and reverse causation must be addressed).
Nested case-control / case-cohort: efficient for costly metabolomics profiling.

Common analytic challenges:

High dimensionality, correlation structures, batch effects, data missingness, and metabolite identification uncertainty.
Confounding and reverse causality (especially in cross-sectional settings).
Reproducibility and portability across platforms and labs (harmonization).



Metabolites can reflect:

Short-term intake (hours-days): for instance, polyphenol metabolites after intake of products rich in these compounds).
Intake patterns (weeks-months): stable patterns that can reflect dietary patterns and macronutrient balance.

A widely used approach is to identify food intake biomarkers from metabolomics-derived molecules and evaluate them on: plausibility and specificity to food, dose-response, intake kinetics, and robustness across populations and platforms. A common practical framework has been to:

Use convential dietary instruments (FFQ or questionnaires) to estimate intake or pattern scores,
Use metabolomics to identify biomarkers or signatures correlated with those exposures,
Validate biomarkers in interventions or independent cohorts,
Use biomarkers to improve the measurement, adherence monitoring and mechanistic inference,
Use these biomarkers in epidemiological analyses to investigater associations with clinical or biological outcomes.

But single metabolites are influenced by multiple factors such as host genetics and physiology, microbiome, physical activity, medication, and disease state, among others. Metabolites are not specific and reflect heterogeneity, therefore there is need for objective biomarkers that capture metabolic adaptation.



Metabolomics can support diet research in different ways:

Exposure validation and calibration
Metabolites can help detect questionnaires misreporting, provide calibration signals alongside classical biomarkers and assess adherence to dietary patterns.
Pathway discovery and mechanistic interpretation
Metabolomics can map metabolism shifts (e.g., amino acid metabolism, lipid remodeling, bile acids, microbiome-linked pathways, inflammatory pathways) relevant to disease-related outcomes.
Pattern recognition
Rather than single nutrients, metabolomics can characterize dietary patterns (e.g., Mediterranean Diet, dietary indices) as multivariate signatures.

Metabolic adaptation to diet is shaped by multiple factors, such as baseline physiology and environment, which motivates multi-marker approaches rather than single metabolites to better represent and summarize the metabolic state.



Precision nutrition aims to deliver dietary guidance tailored to individuals or stratified subgroups based on biological variability (i.e., genetics or epigenetics, lifestyle, exposome, microbiome, sex, ancestry or psychosocial factors). Because this integrates multiple data layers, it often requires advanced statistical learning approaches. Machine learning approaches could be a way to facilitate this prediction and biomarker discovery in the personalized nutrition context.
In this field, metabolomics provides a tool to estimate intake or pattern scores, characterize individuals metabolic state, identify metabolic subtypes responding differently to diets (metabotypes), monitor adherence and biological response and stratify subgroups of individuals who benefit most from specific dietary strategies.

title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Advantages over single metabolites
While single metabolites often lack of specificity and can be noisy, MMS can easily summarize the metabolic complexity and provide a more comprehensive picture of a metabolic state.
Some advantages MMS offer:

increase signal-to-noise by aggregating correlated features,
better capture complex biological relations and pathways,
improve predictive performance and robustness,
offer a scalar score for downstream epidemiological analyses.

title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Penalized regression
Metabolomics data typically contain large number of highly correlated predictors relative to the number of observations (high number of metabolites are measured in a often much smaller sample size). This situation is often referred as high dimensionality of the data (p>>n) and supposes a challange for conventional regression approaches.
Standard multiple regression models often perform poorly under these conditions due to overfitting (where the model captures noise instead of the true biological signal), multicollinearity (as metabolites often belong to shared biochemical pathays and therefore have strong correlations), unstable coefficient estimates (where small changes in the data can lead to large changes in the model parameters).
The Penalized regression methods address these challenges by introducing a regularization penalty to the regression model. This penalty constrains the magnitude of the regression coefficients, shrinking them toward zero (i.e., the model is forced to keep the coefficients small, and therefore less influential). As a result, the model becomes more stable, less prone to overfitting and better predicts high-dimensional settings.
In the context of multi-metabolite signature construction, penalized regression allows the identification of metabolite combinations that jointly predict a dietary exposure or biological phenotype, while accounting for correlations among metabolites.
The general form of penalized regression extends the ordinary least squares objective function by adding a penalty term:





where 𝛌 is a tuning parameter controlling the strength of the penalty and P(𝛃) defines the type of regularization applied to the regression coefficients. The value of 𝛌 is typically determined using cross-validation, which balances model complexity and predictive performance.
Some best practices when performing penalized regressions are to:

Tune hyperparameters via cross-validation,
Standardize predictors,
Utilize external validation (or separate cohort or time-split) when possible.


LASSO
The Least Absolut Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) applies an L1 penalty to the regression coefficients. This shrinks coefficients to zero, performing variable selection.
LASSO is particularly useful when the goal is to identify a sparse set of predictive metabolites, highlighting those most strongly associated with the exposure or outcome.
⚠️In metabolite datasets where many metabolites are strongly associated, LASSO may arbitrarily select one metabolite from a correlated group while excluding others that might be biologically relevant.


Elastic Net
Elastic net combines L1 (LASSO) and L2 (ridge) penalties, allowing to retain groups of correlated predictors while still performing regularization. This approach is particularly well suited for metabolomics data because metabolites within the same biochemical pathway often exhibit strong correlations.
Elastic Net provides a balance between feature selection and coefficient stabilization, and has become one of the most widely used methods for constructing multi-metabolite signatures in nutritional metabolomics studies.


Ridge Regression
Ridge regression applies an L2 penalty, shrinking coefficients toward zero but not forcing them exactly to zero. As a result, all predictors remain in the model but with reduced magnitude.
This approach is particularly useful when many metabolites contribute small but meaningful signals to a biological process. In such situations, ridge regression can produce more stable and reproducible metabolite signatures, especially when predictors are highly correlated. This is the preferred approach if you want to keep all metabolite predictors in the signature, instead of performing a variable selection.

title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Dimension reduction

PCA
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised dimension reduction method that transforms high-dimensional metabolomics data into a smaller set of orthogonal components capturing the major sources of variance. It is widely used for exploratory analysis, including visualization, detection of batch effects, and identification of metabolic clustering or phenotypes.
Each principal component represents a weighted combination of metabolites, and component scores can be calculated for each individual. These scores can be interpreted as metabolite patterns, allowing PCA-derived components to function as unsupervised multi-metabolite signatures. Such metabolite patterns can then be examined in relation to dietary exposures or health outcomes.
In nutritional epidemiology, PCA has been applied to identify metabolite patterns associated with dietary habits. For example, PCA has been used to derive metabolite components from diet-related metabolites, which were subsequently associated with specific food groups using multivariable regression models (Kim et al. 2021).
In the context of multi-metabolite signature (MMS) construction, PCA can also serve as a preprocessing step for dimensionality reduction, for instance by reducing hundreds of metabolites into a smaller set of components that can be used as inputs in predictive models. However, because PCA is unsupervised, the derived components do not necessarily align with a specific exposure or outcome of interest, which may limit their utility for biomarker development compared to supervised approaches.


PLS / PLS-DA
Partial Least Squares (PLS) is a supervised dimension reduction method that identifies latent components by maximizing the covariance between metabolite data and a predefined outcome or exposure. Unlike PCA, which captures overall variance, PLS components are explicitly oriented toward explaining variation that is relevant for a specific biological or dietary variable (Fonville et al. 2010). In the context of metabolomics, PLS is commonly used when the goal is to relate high-dimensional metabolite profiles to continuous outcomes, such as dietary intake or biomarker levels (Yang et al. 2017).
PLS-DA (Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis) is an extension of PLS adapted for categorical outcomes, where the objective is to identify metabolite patterns that discriminate between predefined groups (e.g., high vs low adherence to a dietary pattern, or disease vs control). Both PLS and PLS-DA generate components that represent weighted combinations of metabolites, and individual component scores can be interpreted as multi-metabolite signatures associated with the exposure or classification of interest.
In nutritional metabolomics, PLS-based approaches have been used to derive metabolite patterns associated with dietary exposures and to identify discriminatory metabolic profiles linked to dietary patterns or disease risk. Because these components are optimized for prediction, they often provide more direct biological relevance to the exposure compared to unsupervised methods such as PCA.
However, PLS and especially PLS-DA are prone to overfitting, particularly in high-dimensional settings with limited sample sizes. Therefore, rigorous validation strategies (such as cross-validation, permutation testing, and external validation) are essential to ensure robustness. Additionally, the interpretability of PLS-derived metabolite signatures depends on the stability of component loadings, as unstable weights may limit biological interpretation and reproducibility across studies.

title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Machine learning
Machine-learning methods can be used to construct multi-metabolite signatures when relationships between metabolites and the exposure or outcome may be complex or non-linear. These methods can incorporate a large number of predictors and may capture interactions that are not easily represented by linear regression models.

Random forest

Captures non-linearities and interactions. The variable importance can suggest candidate metabolites.
Needs carful tuning and validation; importance measures can be biased toward certain feature types.



Gradient boosting

Strong predictive performance; handles complex non-linear patterns.
Similar caveats: tuning, calibration, and external validation are crucial.



Support vector machines

Effective in high-dimensional settings; kernel choice controls non-linearity.
Less straightforward interpretability; works best with standardized features and tuned hyperparameters.

title: Scientific context and scope
text:
Scoring frameworks
After selecting the metabolites and estimating their contribution, the information must be combined into a score that can be calculated for each participant. The resulting score summarizes the metabolite profile into a single variable that can be used in validation and downstream epidemiological analyses.

Weighted scores
A weighted multi-metabolite score is commonly calculated by multiplying each metabolite value by its corresponding model coefficient and then summing the resulting values:
[ MMS_i = _{j=1}^{p} j X*{ij}]
where (X_{ij}) is the standardized value of metabolite (j) for participant (i), and (_j) is the weight estimated by the model.
Metabolites with larger coefficients contribute more strongly to the score. Positive and negative coefficients indicate the direction of their contribution.


Metabolite risk scores
A metabolite risk score combines several metabolites associated with a disease outcome or biological risk factor. It is conceptually similar to other composite risk scores, but it uses metabolite concentrations instead of genetic variants or clinical variables.
The score can be examined in relation to disease incidence, clinical biomarkers or other health outcomes. Its predictive value should preferably be evaluated beyond established demographic, lifestyle and clinical risk factors.


Reporting and reproducibility expectations
Clear reporting is important to ensure that a multi-metabolite signature can be understood, reproduced and evaluated in other studies. Ideally, it should include:

the study population and sample size,
metabolomics measurement and quality-control procedures,
variables preprocessing, transformation and standardization;
handling of missing values and batch effects,
the definition of the exposure or outcome,
the method used to divide the data into training and validation sets,
the model, tuning parameters and cross-validation procedure,
the metabolites included in the final signature and their weights,
scores and score calculatoin,
measures of model performance and uncertainty,
the software and packages used in the analysis.

When possible, the analysis code and sufficient information for calculating the signature should be made available. External validation in an independent population is also recommended to assess whether the signature is reproducible and transferable across studies, populations and metabolomics platforms.

title: Welcome
text:
From metabolites to models… and from code to a published website!
This website introduces multi-metabolite signatures (MMS) as an analytical approach for identifying and combining metabolite patterns that reflect external exposures, with a particular focus on diet. These signatures can serve as composite biomarkers to support nutritional epidemiology research and the development and monitoring of dietary strategies for chronic disease prevention.
The website provides a conceptual and practical introduction to building an MMS, covering the main steps from data preprocessing and study design to feature selection, model training, score construction, validation, stability assessment and downstream epidemiological analyses. Reproducible R code accompanies the different stages of the workflow.
This work was developed as part of the Advanced Technologies in Biosciences course during my doctoral studies at Chalmers University of Technology. It brings together work initiated during my Master’s thesis in Bioinformatics and Biostatistics with methods and code that I have learned and applied in nutritional epidemiology projects throughout my PhD.
Developing this resource has strengthened both my theoretical and practical understanding of multi-metabolite signatures. It has also taught me how to build and publish a reproducible Quarto website, a useful way to make scientific methods, explanations and code more accessible and easier to share.
Main learning outcomes:

Understand the principles and applications of multi-metabolite signatures.
Gain hands-on experience in reproducible data analysis and coding.
Learn how to communicate and disseminate scientific methods and code through a Quarto website.

title: Analytical workflow
text:
This page presents a step-by-step workflow for constructing a multimetabolite signature (MMS), covering all key steps from the raw data preparation to the downstream epidemiological applications. The framework is designed to be adaptable across studies.
I hope this offers a useful and inspiring starting point for developing your own MMS workflow! 🧪📊✨

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Data structure
For a supervised MMS approach, the minimum required variables are:






subject identifiers,
metabolomics features,
at least one exposure variable.

Additional elements could be included depending on the study design, such as:

multiple exposures for parallel signature construction,
covariates for adjustment or residualization,
metadata linking feature IDs to metabolite annotations,
downstream outcomes for later epidemiological analyses

For example, consider a substudy of 500 participants, each with a unique subject ID and measured metabolomics data. The metabolomics features could be used as predictors to construct an MMS for a specific exposure, such as the Alternative Healthy Eating Index (AHEI) dietary score. Additional variables, such as age, sex, and BMI, could be included as model covariates, or used in sensitivity analyses. A downstream health outcome, such as incident type 2 diabetes, could then be used in later epidemiological analyses to evaluate whether the MMS is associated with disease risk.
Organise datasets for subsequent analyses
There are several ways to organise datasets for downstream analyses. For example, all variables can be combined into a single dataset, with predictors, covariates, and exposures specified during analysis. Alternatively, the data can be split into separate subsets by type.
The key requirement is that, for the downstream analyses, the predictor matrix (e.g., metabolomics data) is clearly distinguished from exposures, covariates, and other participant-level metadata.
In the workflow example below, I chose to split the data into two datasets: one containing the feature columns used to build the signature, and another containing exposures, outcomes, covariates, and related metadata. I found this structure more convenient, and the helper functions are built with it in mind.






NoteExample code





Variables organisation
# Example: define metabolite feature columns
feature_columns <- colnames(dataset)[feature_start_col:ncol(dataset)]

# Create a dataset with features only
features_df <- dataset[, feature_columns, drop = FALSE]

# Convert feature dataset to model matrix
feature_matrix <- as.matrix(features_df)

# Example: define non-feature variables
exposure_columns <- c("exposure_1")               # replace with your exposure variable(s)
outcome_columns  <- c("outcome_1", "outcome_2")  # replace with your outcome variable(s)
covariate_columns <- c("age", "sex", "bmi")      # replace with your covariates
id_columns <- c("participant_id")                # optional: participant IDs or other metadata

# Create a dataset with participant-level metadata
metadata_df <- dataset[, c(id_columns, exposure_columns, outcome_columns, covariate_columns), drop = FALSE]

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Exposure variables
The target exposure can be a single variable or several related variables if multiple signatures are built in parallel.






NoteExample code





Exposure variables
# Example target exposures for parallel MMS construction
target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = "exposure_a_residual",
  exposure_b = "exposure_b_residual",
  exposure_c = "exposure_c_residual",
  exposure_d = "exposure_d_residual"
)

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Outcome definitions
If the MMS will later be related to disease, mortality, or another endpoint, it is helpful to define those downstream datasets early so the training and testing workflow is explicit.






NoteExample code





Outcome definitions
evaluation_ids <- evaluation_registry_df %>%
  dplyr::pull(participant_id)

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Training and testing subsets
At minimum, an MMS workflow requires both a training and a testing datasets. These can be obtained in two ways:

by using two separate datasets (one for model training and the other for external validation), or
by splitting a single dataset into training and testing subsets (e.g., random split).

In both situations, the training and testing dataset must contain the same variables and be similarly structured.











NoteExample code





User-defined training/test individuals
  # Participants reserved for external or downstream evaluation
evaluation_ids <- external_registry_df %>%
  dplyr::pull(participant_id)

# Training population
train_data <- data %>%
  filter(!participant_id %in% evaluation_ids)

# Testing or external evaluation population
test_data <- data %>%
  filter(participant_id %in% evaluation_ids)




Random training/test splitting helper
# Example helper-based split
split_dataset <- function(data, training_prop = 0.7, strata = NULL) {
  split_obj <- if (is.null(strata)) {
    rsample::initial_split(data, prop = training_prop)
  } else {
    rsample::initial_split(data, prop = training_prop, strata = {{ strata }})
  }

  list(
    split = split_obj,
    train_data = rsample::training(split_obj),
    test_data = rsample::testing(split_obj)
  )
}

# Example use
set.seed(123)

data_split <- split_dataset(
  data = dataset,
  training_prop = 0.7
)

train_data <- data_split$train_data
test_data  <- data_split$test_data










Notestrata





This note refers to the optional strata argument inside split_dataset().
Stratification helps keep the training and testing sets similar with respect to an important variable, usually the outcome or exposure grouping. This makes model training and evaluation more stable and more comparable. For example:

If your outcome is binary and rare, a purely random split might put too few cases in the test set.
If your target has strong class imbalance, stratification preserves roughly the same proportion in both subsets.

Use stratification when:
- you have a categorical outcome like case/control
- you have strong imbalance between groups
- you want both train and test to represent the same population structure
You usually do not need it when:
- the dataset is large and well balanced
- the outcome is continuous and you are doing a simple random split.









Notetraining_prop = 0.7





This note refers to the optional training_prop argument inside split_dataset().
This argument defines the proportion of individuals kept in the training dataset.
If you do not specify it, the default is 0.7, meaning that 70% of individuals are assigned to the training dataset and the remaining 30% to the testing dataset.

title: Analytical workflow
Analytical workflow
text:
Feature selection or exposure residualization
Feature selection is optional and depends on the scientific goal. For ridge regression, all metabolite predictors are retained and coefficients are shrunk, so a separate metabolite-filtering step is usually not required. For LASSO or elastic net, feature selection is part of model fitting because some coefficients may be shrunk to zero.
A common MMS step is not feature selection but exposure residualization. This is useful when the target exposure should represent variation independent of total energy intake, correlated dietary components, demographic characteristics, or other predefined covariates. To avoid leakage, residualization should be fitted in the training data and then applied to the testing data using the same residual model.






NoteExample code





Feature selection
# Example: define metabolite feature columns
feature_columns <- get_feature_columns(
  data = signature_training_df,
  feature_cols = feature_columns
)

# Residualize the exposure using training data only
residualized_exposure_a <- residualize_exposure(
  train_data = signature_training_df,
  new_data = signature_testing_df,
  exposure = "exposure_a",
  covariates = c("total_energy", "age", "sex", "bmi")
)

signature_training_df <- residualized_exposure_a$train_data
signature_testing_df <- residualized_exposure_a$new_data

# Store the residualized exposure name for model training
target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = residualized_exposure_a$residual_name
)

# Optional single-metabolite screening
screening_results <- single_metabolite_screen(
  data = signature_training_df,
  exposure_feature = "exposure_a_residual",
  feature_cols = feature_columns,
  covariates = c("age", "sex", "bmi"),
  correction = "BH"
)

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Model training
In MMS development, several penalized regression approaches can be used depending on the goal of the signature. Ridge regression uses all available metabolite predictors while shrinking their coefficients, which can be useful when metabolites are highly correlated and the aim is to construct a stable multimetabolite score. LASSO encourages sparsity by shrinking some coefficients to zero, making it useful when the goal includes metabolite selection or a more parsimonious signature. Elastic net combines ridge and LASSO penalties, allowing correlated metabolites to be partly retained while still performing some variable selection.
The choice between ridge, LASSO, and elastic net is controlled by the mixture parameter, also known as alpha in glmnet: alpha = 0 corresponds to ridge regression, alpha = 1 corresponds to LASSO, and values between 0 and 1 correspond to elastic net models. For any of these approaches, the penalty parameter should be tuned in the training data using cross-validation. The final MMS model is then fitted in the full training dataset using the selected penalty and applied to new data to generate participant-level MMS scores.






NoteExample code





Model training
target_outcomes <- c(
  exposure_a = "exposure_a_residual",
  exposure_b = "exposure_b_residual",
  exposure_c = "exposure_c_residual"
)

# Fit one ridge MMS model per target exposure
signature_models <- purrr::imap(
  target_outcomes,
  ~ train_mms_model(
    train_data = signature_training_df,
    exposure_feature = .x,
    feature_cols = feature_columns,
    covariates = NULL,
    mixture = 0,
    penalty_levels = 50,
    folds = 10,
    seed = 123,
    normalize_predictors = TRUE
  )
)

# Store selected penalties
best_lambdas <- purrr::map_dbl(
  signature_models,
  ~ .x$best_params$penalty[[1]]
)

# Collect cross-validation performance
cv_metric_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  signature_models,
  ~ .x$metrics %>%
    dplyr::mutate(signature = .y, .before = 1)
)

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Score construction
The MMS score is the model-predicted value for each participant. In other words, once the penalized regression model has learned the weighted combination of metabolites that predicts the target exposure, the predicted value from that model becomes the participant-level MMS. The score can be generated in the testing dataset, the full study dataset, or an external validation dataset as long as the same preprocessing and model object are used.






NoteExample code





Score construction
# Generate MMS scores in the testing dataset
signature_testing_results <- signature_testing_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  signature_testing_results <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = signature_testing_results,
    score_name = score_name
  )
}

# Generate MMS scores in the full analysis dataset
analysis_with_scores <- analysis_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  analysis_with_scores <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = analysis_with_scores,
    score_name = score_name
  )
}

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Score standardization
MMS scores are often standardized so that downstream estimates are interpreted per one standard deviation of the signature. The reference distribution should be defined clearly. For internal validation, the testing set can be standardized within itself. For transportability or comparison across datasets, it is usually better to standardize using the training-set score distribution and apply the same mean and standard deviation to the testing or downstream dataset.






NoteExample code





MMS score standardization
# First generate training scores to define the reference distribution
signature_training_results <- signature_training_df

for (signature_name in names(signature_models)) {
  score_name <- paste0("signature_score_", signature_name)

  signature_training_results <- predict_mms_score(
    model_object = signature_models[[signature_name]],
    new_data = signature_training_results,
    score_name = score_name
  )

  signature_testing_results <- standardize_from_reference(
    data = signature_testing_results,
    score_col = score_name,
    reference_data = signature_training_results,
    new_col = paste0(score_name, "_sd")
  )

  analysis_with_scores <- standardize_from_reference(
    data = analysis_with_scores,
    score_col = score_name,
    reference_data = signature_training_results,
    new_col = paste0(score_name, "_sd")
  )
}

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Weighted metabolite scores
The predicted values from the penalized model become the MMS score. These can then be standardized for interpretation per standard deviation.






NoteExample code





Weighted metabolite scores
all_signature_scores <- purrr::imap(
  signature_models,
  ~ predict_train_model(.x, analysis_df)
)

analysis_df <- dplyr::bind_cols(
  analysis_df,
  purrr::set_names(as.data.frame(all_signature_scores), paste0("signature_score_", names(all_signature_scores)))
) %>%
  mutate(across(starts_with("signature_score_"), scale, .names = "{.col}_sd"))

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Pediction performance
Model evaluation evaluates whether the MMS score reproduces the target exposure in participants who were not used to train the model. For continuous exposures, useful validation metrics include R^2, RMSE, MAE, and the regression slope from a model of the observed or residualized exposure on the MMS score.

R², calibration slope RMSE and MAE
R^2 quantifies the proportion of variation in the target exposure explained by the MMS score in the testing dataset. RMSE and MAE summarize prediction error: RMSE penalizes larger errors more strongly, while MAE represents the average absolute difference between the observed exposure and the MMS-predicted exposure. These metrics are most interpretable when the observed exposure and MMS score are on the same scale. When both variables are standardized, the regression slope can also be interpreted as the expected SD difference in the target exposure per one SD higher MMS.






NoteExample code





Model performance
evaluate_mms_performance <- function(data,
                                     truth,
                                     estimate,
                                     signature_name = NULL) {
  eval_df <- data %>%
    dplyr::select(
      truth = dplyr::all_of(truth),
      estimate = dplyr::all_of(estimate)
    ) %>%
    tidyr::drop_na()

  fit <- stats::lm(truth ~ estimate, data = eval_df)

  slope <- broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
    dplyr::filter(term == "estimate")

  fit_summary <- broom::glance(fit)

  tibble::tibble(
    signature = signature_name,
    n = nrow(eval_df),

    # Regression-based validation
    beta = slope$estimate,
    conf.low = slope$conf.low,
    conf.high = slope$conf.high,
    p.value = slope$p.value,
    r_squared = fit_summary$r.squared,
    adj_r_squared = fit_summary$adj.r.squared,

    # Prediction-error metrics
    rmse = yardstick::rmse_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    ),
    mae = yardstick::mae_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    ),
    rsq_yardstick = yardstick::rsq_vec(
      truth = eval_df$truth,
      estimate = eval_df$estimate
    )
  )
}

If the MMS score and target exposure have been standardized using the same reference distribution, RMSE and MAE are expressed in SD units. This can make performance easier to compare across different exposure signatures. The standardization approach should be reported clearly, especially if MMS scores are later used in downstream epidemiological models.

title: Analytical workflow
text:
Cross-validation results
Cross-validation results summarize how the MMS model performed during training and how stable the fitted model was across resampling folds. These results are useful for reporting the selected penalty, comparing model families, and assessing whether the signature is driven by consistent metabolite contributions rather than by a small number of unstable features.
For penalized regression models, the most relevant cross-validation outputs are usually the selected penalty parameter, the cross-validated performance metrics, and the distribution of metabolite coefficients across folds. Ridge regression usually retains all metabolite predictors with non-zero coefficients, so coefficient magnitude and rank stability are often more informative than selection frequency. In contrast, for LASSO or elastic net models, selection frequency can be interpreted as the proportion of folds in which each metabolite was retained with a non-zero coefficient.

Cross-validation results
summarize_cv_performance <- function(model_object, signature_name = NULL) {
  model_object$metrics %>%
    dplyr::filter(.metric %in% c("rmse", "mae", "rsq")) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      signature = signature_name,
      selected_penalty = model_object$best_params$penalty[[1]],
      mixture = model_object$mixture,
      .before = 1
    )
}

cv_performance_table <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  signature_models,
  ~ summarize_cv_performance(.x, signature_name = .y)
)


summarize_cv_coefficients <- function(model_object, feature_annotation_df = NULL) {
  recipe_obj <- workflows::extract_recipe(model_object$final_fit)
  penalty_value <- model_object$best_params$penalty[[1]]
  exposure_feature <- model_object$exposure_feature
  mixture_value <- model_object$mixture

  fold_coefficients <- purrr::map(model_object$folds$splits, function(split) {
    fold_training_df <- rsample::analysis(split)

    prepped_recipe <- recipes::prep(
      recipe_obj,
      training = fold_training_df,
      retain = TRUE
    )

    baked_fold <- recipes::juice(prepped_recipe)

    x_fold <- baked_fold %>%
      dplyr::select(-dplyr::all_of(exposure_feature)) %>%
      as.matrix()

    y_fold <- baked_fold[[exposure_feature]]

    glmnet::glmnet(
      x = x_fold,
      y = y_fold,
      alpha = mixture_value,
      lambda = penalty_value
    ) %>%
      stats::coef() %>%
      as.matrix()
  })

  coefficient_df <- do.call(cbind, fold_coefficients)
  colnames(coefficient_df) <- paste0("fold_", seq_len(ncol(coefficient_df)))

  coefficient_summary <- as.data.frame(coefficient_df) %>%
    tibble::rownames_to_column("feature_id") %>%
    dplyr::filter(feature_id != "(Intercept)") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      median = apply(dplyr::pick(dplyr::starts_with("fold_")), 1, stats::median),
      q1 = apply(dplyr::pick(dplyr::starts_with("fold_")), 1, stats::quantile, probs = 0.25),
      q3 = apply(dplyr::pick(dplyr::starts_with("fold_")), 1, stats::quantile, probs = 0.75),
      selection_frequency = rowMeans(dplyr::pick(dplyr::starts_with("fold_")) != 0)
    )

  if (!is.null(feature_annotation_df)) {
    coefficient_summary <- coefficient_summary %>%
      dplyr::left_join(feature_annotation_df, by = "feature_id")
  }

  coefficient_summary
}

coefficient_summary_list <- purrr::imap(
  signature_models,
  ~ summarize_cv_coefficients(.x, feature_annotation_df = feature_annotation_df)
)
